deck.title: Modern interview practice
deck.description: 30 original exercises for mid-level SWE preparation: 18 core algorithms in current engineering contexts, 4 JavaScript/Python semantics and concurrency problems, and 8 practical design discussions. Practice clarifying, reasoning, coding, testing, and explaining trade-offs. Designed to complement preparation for roles such as Google L4; not official Google material, actual interview questions, or a guarantee of any interview format. Confirm role-specific expectations with your recruiter.

cards.title: Deduplicate a retrying event stream
cards.question:
A telemetry collector receives [timestamp, eventId] pairs in timestamp order. Accept an event only if that ID has not been accepted during the preceding window seconds. Return one boolean per arrival.

Contract

  • Timestamps are nonnegative integers in nondecreasing order; event IDs are strings.
  • window is positive. An acceptance at time a expires at a + window; a retry exactly then is accepted.
  • Rejected retries do not refresh the expiry. Process a finite batch of at most 100,000 events.

Examples to reason through

  • [[0,'a'],[2,'a'],[5,'a']], window=5 → [true,false,true].
  • [[0,'a'],[0,'b'],[0,'a']], window=1 → [true,true,false].
cards.answer:
Keep each ID's last accepted timestamp in a hash map. A later arrival is accepted when the ID is absent or its last acceptance is at least window seconds old. Update only on acceptance. This batch implementation keeps one entry per distinct ID; a production unbounded stream also needs expiry cleanup.

Complexity: Expected O(n) time and O(u) auxiliary space for n arrivals and u distinct IDs, assuming expected constant-time hash operations; output uses O(n).

cards.title: Smallest incident evidence window
cards.question:
An incident timeline is an array of signal names. Find the shortest contiguous interval containing every distinct required signal at least once. Return [start, endExclusive], breaking ties by the earliest start, or null/None if impossible.

Contract

  • Signal names are strings; required is interpreted as a set.
  • Empty required returns [0,0]. There are at most 100,000 timeline entries.

Examples to reason through

  • ['ok','timeout','retry','ok','timeout'], required=['timeout','retry'] → [1,3].
  • ['ok'], required=['timeout'] → null/None; empty required → [0,0].
cards.answer:
Expand the right edge, counting required signals and how many distinct requirements are present. While all are present, record the window if strictly shorter, then shrink the left edge. Each edge moves only forward, so every timeline entry enters and leaves at most once.

Complexity: Expected O(n + r) time, O(r) auxiliary space, for n signals and r required entries.

cards.title: Top error categories with deterministic ties
cards.question:
Return the k most frequent error codes in a batch. Order by descending frequency, then ascending ASCII code string so two replicas produce the same report.

Contract

  • Error codes are ASCII strings. k is an integer ≥ 0.
  • Return all distinct codes when k exceeds their count. Input order must remain unchanged.

Examples to reason through

  • ['503','429','503','404','429'], k=2 → ['429','503'].
  • Empty input or k=0 → []; ['x','x','a'], k=9 → ['x','a'].
cards.answer:
Count into a map, then sort distinct codes with the complete ranking rule. The straightforward solution is easy to verify and appropriate when the number of categories is small. A size-k heap is a useful optimization when the distinct count is much larger than k.

Complexity: Expected O(n + u log u) time and O(u) auxiliary space for n codes and u distinct values; treats code length as bounded.

cards.title: Reassemble uploaded byte ranges
cards.question:
A resumable upload has received half-open byte ranges [start,end). Merge overlapping or touching ranges and return their sorted union. Also explain how the union reveals gaps in an upload of known total size.

Contract

  • Bounds are integers with 0 ≤ start ≤ end. Zero-length ranges add no bytes.
  • Ranges may be unsorted or duplicated. Do not mutate the input.

Examples to reason through

  • [[4,8],[0,3],[3,5],[10,12]] → [[0,8],[10,12]].
  • [[2,2],[1,4],[2,3],[1,4]] → [[1,4]].
cards.answer:
Sort nonempty copies by start. The union's final range is the only range that can overlap the next input range. Extend its end when the next start is at most that end; otherwise append a new range. Gaps lie before the first range, between merged ranges, and after the last range up to total size.

Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary space including copied ranges and output.

sections.title: Worked approach
sections.html: Sort nonempty copies by start. The union's final range is the only range that can overlap the next input range. Extend its end when the next start is at most that end; otherwise append a new range. Gaps lie before the first range, between merged ranges, and after the last range up to total size.

cards.title: Find the shortest service dependency chain
cards.question:
A directed graph maps a service to the services it directly calls. Return a shortest path from source to target measured in call hops, or an empty list if unreachable.

Contract

  • Service names are strings. Missing adjacency entries mean no outgoing edges.
  • Cycles and duplicate edges are allowed. Any shortest path is acceptable; traverse neighbors in input order for deterministic output.

Examples to reason through

  • a→[b,c], b→[d], c→[d], source=a,target=d → [a,b,d].
  • source=target → [source], even with no adjacency entry; unreachable → [].
cards.answer:
Breadth-first search visits vertices in nondecreasing hop distance. Mark vertices when enqueued and store one parent per vertex. Once the target is dequeued, follow parents backward and reverse the path. Storing complete paths in the queue would waste space.

Complexity: Expected O(V + E) time and O(V) auxiliary space for reachable vertices and examined edges.

cards.title: Order a deployment dependency graph
cards.question:
Given n deployment jobs numbered 0 through n−1 and edges [prerequisite,dependent], return a valid execution order. Return null/None if there is a cycle.

Contract

  • All endpoints are valid job indices. Duplicate dependency edges are allowed and should be harmless.
  • Any valid ordering is acceptable. Empty jobs return [].

Examples to reason through

  • n=4, edges=[[0,2],[1,2],[2,3]] → [0,1,2,3].
  • n=2, edges=[[0,1],[1,0]] → null/None.
cards.answer:
Count incoming edges, enqueue every zero-indegree job, then remove its outgoing edges as it is processed. A newly zero-indegree job is ready. If fewer than n jobs are emitted, some jobs remain in a cycle or depend on one. Counting and later decrementing duplicate edges consistently preserves correctness.

Complexity: O(V + E) time and O(V + E) space including the adjacency list.

python.code:
from collections import deque

def deployment_order(n, edges):
    out = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    degree = [0] * n
    for a, b in edges:
        out[a].append(b)
        degree[b] += 1
    queue = deque(i for i in range(n) if degree[i] == 0)
    result = []
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        result.append(node)
        for nxt in out[node]:
            degree[nxt] -= 1
            if degree[nxt] == 0:
                queue.append(nxt)
    return result if len(result) == n else None
python.testCode:
assert deployment_order(4,[[0,2],[1,2],[2,3]]) == [0,1,2,3]
assert deployment_order(2,[[0,1],[1,0]]) is None
assert deployment_order(1,[[0,0]]) is None
assert deployment_order(2,[[0,1],[0,1]]) == [0,1]
assert deployment_order(0,[]) == []
python.complexity: O(V + E) time and O(V + E) space including the adjacency list.

cards.title: Find the least-latency service route
cards.question:
Given a directed graph of n nodes and edges [from,to,latency], return the minimum total latency from source to target, or null/None if no route exists.

Contract

  • Latencies are nonnegative integers. All path sums fit in JavaScript's safe integer range.
  • Nodes are 0…n−1; source and target are valid. Parallel edges and zero-cost edges are permitted.

Examples to reason through

  • n=3, edges=[[0,1,8],[0,2,2],[2,1,1]], source=0,target=1 → 3.
  • source=target → 0; disconnected target → null/None.
cards.answer:
Use Dijkstra's algorithm with a min-heap of tentative distances. An improved distance pushes a new entry; skip stale entries when popped. The smallest non-stale distance is final because remaining edges cannot reduce it. Return only when the target is popped, not when first discovered.

Complexity: O(V + E log(E+1)) time and O(V + E) space for this lazy-duplicate heap implementation.

cards.title: An LRU cache for feature metadata
cards.question:
Implement an LRU cache supporting get(key) and put(key,value). A successful get or put makes that key most recently used. Evict the least recently used key when capacity is exceeded.

Contract

  • Capacity is a nonnegative integer. Keys are strings and stored values are non-null strings or numbers.
  • A miss returns null/None. Updating an existing key must not evict another key. Capacity zero stores nothing.

Examples to reason through

  • capacity=2: put(a,1), put(b,2), get(a), put(c,3), get(b) → 1 then null/None.
  • capacity=0: put(a,1), get(a) → null/None.
cards.answer:
Maintain keys from least to most recently used. On a hit or update, move the key to the end; after insertion, remove the first key if over capacity. JavaScript Map preserves insertion order, so delete and reinsert explicitly. Python OrderedDict provides move_to_end and popitem(last=False). For a strict data-structure exercise, implement a hash table plus a doubly linked list.

Complexity: O(capacity) space. Operations are expected O(1) on typical hash-backed implementations; ECMAScript requires average sublinear Map access, not a strict O(1) guarantee.

cards.title: Rolling peak request latency
cards.question:
Given request latencies and a window width k, return the maximum latency in every contiguous window of k requests.

Contract

  • 1 ≤ k ≤ len(values); empty input with k=0 returns []. Invalid widths raise an error.
  • Values are finite numbers. Do not mutate the input.

Examples to reason through

  • [8,3,5,9,2], k=3 → [8,9,9].
  • [4,4,4], k=2 → [4,4]; [1,2], k=1 → [1,2].
cards.answer:
Store candidate indices in a deque with decreasing values. Expire indices outside the window; remove smaller or equal values from the back because the new value is at least as useful and expires later. The front is each window's maximum. Each index is added and removed once.

Complexity: Amortized O(n) time, O(k) auxiliary queue space, plus O(n−k+1) output.

cards.title: Fit a conversation into a token budget
cards.question:
A conversation has per-message token costs. Find the longest contiguous block whose total cost is at most budget. Return [start,endExclusive], preferring the earliest block on ties.

Contract

  • Costs and budget are nonnegative integers; sums fit in JavaScript's safe integer range.
  • You may return [0,0] if no nonempty block fits. This is a toy token-budget problem, not a tokenizer implementation.

Examples to reason through

  • [4,2,1,5,1], budget=7 → [0,3].
  • [0,0,2], budget=0 → [0,2]; [8], budget=3 → [0,0].
cards.answer:
Expand the right edge and keep the window's running sum. If over budget, advance the left edge until feasible. Nonnegative costs make this safe: removing a prefix cannot increase the sum, and an infeasible prefix cannot become feasible by extending it. Record strictly longer windows to preserve the earliest tie.

Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

cards.title: Merge regional audit streams
cards.question:
Each region provides an ascending array of integer event timestamps. Merge all arrays into one ascending timeline, preserving duplicates.

Contract

  • Each input array is already sorted. There can be empty regions or no regions.
  • Return timestamps only; a production event record would also need a stable tie-break key. Do not mutate inputs.

Examples to reason through

  • [[1,4,9],[1,3],[],[2,8]] → [1,1,2,3,4,8,9].
  • [] → []; [[5,5]] → [5,5].
cards.answer:
Put the first item from each nonempty stream in a min-heap together with its stream and item index. Pop the smallest, append it, then push only its successor. At every step the heap contains the smallest unconsumed item from each stream, so the global minimum must be in the heap.

Complexity: O(K + N log(K+1)) time, O(K) auxiliary heap space plus O(N) output, for K streams and N items.

import heapq

def merge_streams(streams):
    heap = [(stream[0],s,0) for s,stream in enumerate(streams) if stream]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    result = []
    while heap:
        value,s,i = heapq.heappop(heap)
        result.append(value)
        if i+1 < len(streams[s]):
            heapq.heappush(heap,(streams[s][i+1],s,i+1))
    return result

cards.question:
A configuration registry assigns a value to each string prefix. Build a trie and return the value for the longest stored prefix of a query, or null/None when no prefix matches.

Contract

  • Prefixes and queries are ASCII strings; values are non-null strings. This is raw string-prefix matching, not URL routing or path normalization.
  • An empty prefix is a default. Later inserts replace values at the exact same prefix.

  • Prefixes [('', 'default'), ('api/', 'shared'), ('api/pay/', 'payments')], query='api/pay/create' → 'payments'.

Each trie edge consumes one character. Store values only at completed prefixes. Traverse the query while remembering the last value encountered; stopping at a missing edge preserves the deepest matching prefix. Separate the missing-value sentinel from legitimate values.

cards.title: Group connected devices
cards.question:
An internal inventory lists n device indices and trusted pairwise links that indicate devices belong to the same diagnostic group. Return every connected component, with members and components in ascending index order.

Contract

  • Devices are 0…n−1, and links are undirected. Isolated devices form one-member groups.
  • Links are already authorized inventory data; this task does not infer personal identity. Duplicate links and self-links are allowed.

Examples to reason through

  • n=6, links=[[0,2],[2,4],[1,3]] → [[0,2,4],[1,3],[5]].
  • n=0 → []; n=2, links=[[0,0],[0,1],[0,1]] → [[0,1]].
cards.answer:
Use disjoint-set union with path compression and union by size. Union each pair, then visit device indices in increasing order and append each device to its root's group. The first encounter with a component is its smallest index, so insertion-ordered group maps already provide the required component order.

Complexity: O((n+m) α(n)) amortized time and O(n) space for m links, where α is the inverse Ackermann function.

cards.title: Choose a worker's minimum batch capacity
cards.question:
Jobs arrive in a fixed order with positive integer costs. A worker processes a contiguous prefix of remaining jobs per batch, with total cost at most capacity. Find the minimum integer capacity that completes all jobs in at most batches batches.

Contract

  • batches is a positive integer. A job cannot be split or reordered.
  • All sums fit in JavaScript's safe integer range. Empty jobs return zero.

Examples to reason through

  • costs=[7,2,5,10,8], batches=2 → 18, using [7,2,5] and [10,8].
  • costs=[3,4], batches=9 → 4; batches=1 → 7.
cards.answer:
For a proposed capacity, greedily fill each batch before starting another. This uses the fewest possible batches for that capacity. Feasibility is monotone: more capacity never requires more batches. Binary-search between the largest job and the total cost using the predicate neededBatches ≤ batches.

Complexity: O(n log(S+1)) time and O(1) auxiliary space, where S is total cost.

cards.question:
A usage ledger contains signed deltas: consumption is positive and refunds are negative. Count contiguous nonempty intervals whose net usage equals target.

Contract

  • Deltas and target are integers with absolute value ≤ 1,000,000. Input length ≤ 100,000, so sums, differences, and counts fit in JavaScript's safe integer range.

Query before inserting the current sum so empty intervals are excluded. A sliding window fails with negative deltas.

cards.question:
A compact identifier is formed by concatenating dictionary tokens. Return any segmentation into the fewest tokens, or null/None if no segmentation exists.

cards.question:
Each maintenance job has a half-open interval [start,end). Choose the maximum number of jobs that can run on one exclusive maintenance lane, and return their original indices in scheduled order.

Contract

  • Each start is strictly less than its end. Touching jobs are compatible.

Implement mapSettledLimit(items, limit, asyncFn). Run at most limit calls at once, continue after failures, and return outcomes in input order as {status:'fulfilled',value} or {status:'rejected',reason:string}.

cards.title: Design an offline-first review app
cards.question:
Design a study app that remains useful on a phone during a week without connectivity, then reconciles progress across two devices. Explain storage, synchronization, conflict behavior, and updates.

Requirements

  • Reading downloaded decks and recording reviews must work offline after initial installation/download.
  • A review must not disappear or be counted twice after reconnecting. Note edits from two devices must not silently overwrite each other.
  • Users need a visible download state, pending-sync count, and portable export.

Assumed scale

Assume 50,000 daily active users × 200 reviews/day = 10 million review events/day, about 116/s average and 1,200/s at a 10× peak. At 256 bytes/event, raw events are about 2.56 GB/day before indexes and replication. A typical device caches 20 MB of deck data.
cards.answer:
Separate immutable deck assets, local user state, and a durable outbox of pending operations. The app renders from local state immediately and synchronizes in the background when it can.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Draw two separate flows: the local transaction and the later server acknowledgement. Identify which side owns each identifier and cursor.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Separate immutable deck assets, local user state, and a durable outbox of pending operations. The app renders from local state immediately and synchronizes in the background when it can.
  • Use a service worker to cache a versioned application shell/deck assets and IndexedDB for structured progress plus the outbox. Commit the local review and its outbox event in one transaction. Display a ready-for-offline status only after required assets are cached.
  • Give each operation a device-generated unique ID and tenant/user scope. POST batches with these IDs; the server deduplicates transactionally, assigns a monotone server sequence, and returns acknowledgements plus a pull cursor. Delete acknowledged outbox entries only after their acknowledgements are durable locally.
  • Model reviews as append-only events so concurrent devices can both contribute. State a deterministic scheduling policy: for example, process accepted review events in server sequence order and recompute the card schedule. Device timestamps remain display metadata because clocks can disagree. Deduplication removes retries, not genuinely separate reviews.
  • For notes, send the base revision. If it is stale, retain both versions and offer a merge instead of last-write-wins data loss. Keep deck content version separate from progress IDs so a content update does not reset learning history.
  • Coordinate shell/deck/schema upgrades, provide a recoverable export, and test storage eviction. A browser can remove local data; offline storage alone is not a backup. Reauthenticate on reconnect, scope caches by account, and clear private local data on an explicit sign-out policy.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• An append-only review log simplifies retry handling and auditability but needs compaction/checkpoints for long histories.
  • Automatic conflict resolution feels smooth but needs a product rule; preserving both note edits is safer when intent cannot be inferred.
  • Download-on-demand reduces storage; downloading all chosen decks gives a stronger offline promise. Background execution differs by mobile platform, so sync-on-open must work.

sections.html:
• Kill the app between local write and upload, and between server commit and response; repeated uploads must converge without missing reviews.
  • Edit the same note on two offline devices, skew a device clock, update the deck while offline, and exhaust storage.
  • Install online, confirm caching, disable all network, reopen from the home screen, review cards, then reconnect and verify counts.

• Make (tenant_id, idempotency_key) a unique database key. Store a canonical request digest, job ID, creation status, and expiry. Authenticate and authorize before lookup; the key is not an authorization token.

sections.html:
• Persisting the original response provides exact replay but uses more storage than retaining a canonical resource ID.

  • A distributed cache can speed lookup, but correctness should live in an atomic durable boundary, with careful expiry semantics.

• Fire 100 simultaneous same-key requests; assert one job row and one logical execution.

cards.title: Protect a multi-tenant API from bursts
cards.question:
Design per-tenant admission control for a shared API. A tenant should sustain 100 requests/s and briefly burst to 200 requests without overwhelming shared backends.

Requirements

  • Return a clear rejection response and useful retry guidance when the tenant budget is exhausted.
  • Protect the backend with a global concurrency/load limit as well as per-tenant fairness.
  • Explain behavior during limiter failure and across two regions.

Assumed scale

Assume 1,000 active tenants and 20,000 incoming requests/s total, with heavily skewed traffic. A typical admitted request holds backend resources for 100 ms; 20,000 requests/s at that mean duration implies roughly 2,000 concurrent requests before queues and overhead.
cards.answer:
Use one token bucket per tenant: capacity 200, refill 100 tokens/s. On arrival, refill by elapsed time up to capacity, then atomically consume one token if available. Store balance and last-refill time together at the limiter's authoritative shard.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Write the bucket state and atomic update first. Then identify the guarantee lost when you add replicas or fallbacks.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Use one token bucket per tenant: capacity 200, refill 100 tokens/s. On arrival, refill by elapsed time up to capacity, then atomically consume one token if available. Store balance and last-refill time together at the limiter's authoritative shard.
  • Use a single atomic operation or server-side script for read/refill/decrement; separate reads and writes overspend under concurrency. Base elapsed time on a consistent server clock and clamp negative elapsed time. Expire inactive buckets only after enough time to refill fully.
  • A depleted bucket returns HTTP 429 with a retry delay derived from the deficit. Clients apply bounded backoff with jitter. Rate limiting does not replace a concurrency cap, bounded queue, deadlines, or shedding low-priority work under backend overload.
  • Choose failure behavior by endpoint: strict fail-closed for costly scarce operations; a small local emergency allowance for a read endpoint that can tolerate bounded overshoot. Record fallback activations and make the overshoot bound explicit.
  • For two regions, either route a tenant to one authoritative bucket, coordinate globally at added latency, or allocate regional quotas whose sum stays within the global budget. Independently issuing the full quota in both regions doubles the allowed rate. Rebalancing quota requires careful ownership and failure handling.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• Central coordination strengthens the global limit but adds latency and a dependency; local buckets are faster but can overshoot.
  • Token buckets permit controlled bursts; sliding logs track exact recent arrivals but cost more memory and work.
  • A tenant's rate is only one dimension: request cost, active streams, or tokens may be more meaningful than raw request count.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Send simultaneous requests at refill boundaries, idle then burst, skew clocks, and fail the authoritative shard.
  • Create one hot tenant, rebalance regions, and prove the maximum overshoot under fallback.
  • Measure admitted/rejected requests by bounded labels, limiter latency, backend saturation, and queue age.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: Support weighted requests, tenant priorities, long-lived streaming calls, or a limit that must never be exceeded globally.

sections.title: Self-review rubric
sections.html:
• Derives refill and burst behavior and includes atomicity.
  • Distinguishes rate, concurrency, queue length, and overload.
  • Quantifies the consistency/failure trade-off instead of assuming global correctness from local counters.

cards.title: Deliver webhooks despite retries and outages
cards.question:
Design a webhook delivery service that accepts tenant events, reliably attempts delivery to registered destinations, and tolerates duplicates, slow receivers, and multi-hour outages.

Requirements

  • Persist events before acknowledging acceptance. Retry transient failures with bounded backoff; preserve terminal failures for inspection/replay.
  • Give each event a stable delivery identity and authenticate payloads.
  • Do not claim exactly-once business side effects at an arbitrary receiver.

Assumed scale

Assume 500 events/s × 1 KB/event = about 43.2 GB/day of raw payloads. A six-hour destination outage can accumulate 10.8 million events if all traffic targets it; isolate that backlog so healthy tenants continue.
cards.answer:
Accept the event into durable storage and enqueue an event reference through a transaction/outbox boundary. Partition work by tenant or destination and enforce per-destination concurrency so one slow endpoint cannot occupy the entire worker fleet.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Walk through the ambiguous outcome after a receiver commits but the sender times out. No broker setting can remove that ambiguity by itself.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Accept the event into durable storage and enqueue an event reference through a transaction/outbox boundary. Partition work by tenant or destination and enforce per-destination concurrency so one slow endpoint cannot occupy the entire worker fleet.
  • A worker acquires a bounded lease, signs the payload with a rotating destination secret, and sends a stable event ID plus a timestamp. Apply connection and total deadlines, response-size limits, and a configured egress policy for registered URLs.
  • Mark success on the agreed successful response range. Retry network errors, timeouts, and selected retryable statuses with exponential backoff and jitter; honor bounded retry guidance. Cap attempts or event age, then move the record to an inspectable failed state. Do not retry every permanent 4xx indefinitely.
  • If a receiver commits and its acknowledgement is lost, the sender cannot know whether processing happened. It must retry and the receiver should deduplicate the stable event ID in the same transaction as its business update. A queue's exactly-once feature has a specific scope and does not make arbitrary HTTP effects exactly once.
  • Expose delivery attempts, next retry, and a controlled replay API. Monitor oldest backlog age, success rate, attempt amplification, per-destination latency, and failed-event count. Preserve ordering only where required; strict ordering can let one poison event block later ones.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• At-least-once delivery is recoverable but requires duplicate-tolerant consumers. At-most-once avoids retries but can lose events.
  • Per-destination ordering simplifies some consumers and reduces throughput/availability when a message fails.
  • Long retention helps recovery but consumes storage and may retain sensitive payloads; store only what the product needs.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Kill a worker after the receiver accepts but before local acknowledgement; expect a duplicate with the same ID.
  • Simulate 429, 500, a permanent 400, a hanging response, secret rotation, and an invalid registered destination.
  • Drain a large backlog without starving new traffic or unrelated tenants; replay must retain a deliberate deduplication policy.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: How would you handle per-user ordering, schema evolution, destination deletion, and receiver-managed replay cursors?

sections.html:
• Identifies the durable acknowledgement boundary and lease/retry policy.
  • Explains duplicate handling end to end, with correct scope for guarantees.
  • Prevents one tenant or poison event from exhausting shared resources.

cards.title: Paginate a changing activity feed
cards.question:
Design a paginated tenant activity feed that remains efficient deep into a large history while new events arrive. Explain cursor contents, ordering, permissions, and what consistency the client gets.

Requirements

  • Return up to 50 rows per page, newest first, with an opaque next-page token.
  • Support a fixed tenant and event-type filter across a traversal.
  • Define behavior for inserts and deletions during pagination; do not promise a snapshot accidentally.

Assumed scale

Assume 50 million retained rows, 2,000 list requests/s, and a target p95 under 150 ms. Rows have immutable created_at and a unique ID; many rows share the same timestamp.
cards.answer:
Define a total order (created_at DESC, id DESC). For a page after cursor (t,id), query rows whose tuple is smaller, with the same tenant/filter, ordered by the same keys, LIMIT pageSize+1. The extra row determines whether another page exists.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Choose a unique stable ordering before designing the token. A timestamp alone is not enough.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Define a total order (created_at DESC, id DESC). For a page after cursor (t,id), query rows whose tuple is smaller, with the same tenant/filter, ordered by the same keys, LIMIT pageSize+1. The extra row determines whether another page exists.
  • Use an index beginning with the equality predicates such as (tenant_id,event_type,created_at DESC,id DESC), adjusting to actual query patterns. Large OFFSET values require the database to find and skip earlier rows; keyset pagination seeks near the cursor instead.
  • Encode the last returned tuple, normalized filter/version, tenant scope, expiry, and optionally a traversal high-water mark in a signed opaque token. Validate size and version; reject changed filters. The token is a continuation mechanism, not authorization: check access on every request.
  • Choose a moving-view guarantee: new higher-ranked rows appear on refresh, not in later pages. Deletions may shorten pages. Immutable order keys avoid moving existing rows across the boundary. A first-page high-water mark can exclude later high-ranked inserts but does not provide a full snapshot when rows can be deleted or backfilled.
  • If a stable export is required, create a snapshot/materialized export job with its own lifecycle instead of holding a database transaction open across a user's long browsing session. Bound page size, token lifetime, query timeout, and allowed filters.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• Keyset pagination supports efficient sequential traversal but cannot cheaply jump to arbitrary page 1,000.
  • Opaque tokens let the backend evolve; exposing raw offsets or database keys as a public contract makes migrations harder.
  • A moving feed prioritizes fresh data and low cost. Stable historical exports need stronger snapshot semantics and storage.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Use many equal timestamps, insert new rows between pages, delete the last row from a prior page, and change permissions mid-traversal.
  • Tamper with the token, change filters, use an expired token, and try a token from another tenant.
  • Measure deep-page plans and latency with realistic skew; verify no duplicate rows when immutable keys and a fixed query are used.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: Add reverse pagination, full-text ranking, multi-region writes, or a legally auditable point-in-time export.

sections.title: Self-review rubric
sections.html:
• Uses a unique order and matching seek predicate/index.
  • Binds tokens to query context while rechecking permissions.
  • States the actual consistency contract for concurrent changes.

cards.title: Prevent a hot-key cache stampede
cards.question:
A read API uses cache-aside metadata caching. When a popular key expires, thousands of requests hit the origin simultaneously. Design a recovery path that protects the origin and returns appropriately fresh data.

Requirements

  • For this exercise, metadata may be stale for at most 60 seconds after its freshness TTL; authorization decisions may not use this stale policy.
  • A failed refresh must not create an unbounded request pile-up.
  • Explain local versus fleet-wide request coalescing and data updates racing with refreshes.

Assumed scale

Assume 15,000 reads/s, an origin sustainable capacity of 2,000 reads/s, and one hot key receiving 1,000 reads/s. An origin refresh takes 200 ms, so an uncoalesced miss burst can create roughly 200 simultaneous refreshes for that one key.
cards.answer:
Store value, source version, fresh-until, and stale-until. Fresh entries return immediately. A stale-but-allowed entry returns its value while triggering a refresh. After stale-until, either wait within a short bound for a refresh or fail according to the endpoint's contract.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Separate fresh, stale-but-allowed, and unusable states. Then decide who may refresh each state and for how long.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Store value, source version, fresh-until, and stale-until. Fresh entries return immediately. A stale-but-allowed entry returns its value while triggering a refresh. After stale-until, either wait within a short bound for a refresh or fail according to the endpoint's contract.
  • Coalesce same-key refreshes within each process using a pending promise/task. For fleet-wide protection, use a bounded distributed lease or a dedicated refresh worker so many processes do not each call the origin. A lease is an optimization: its expiry may allow overlapping refreshes.
  • Write refreshed values only if their source version is at least the stored version, or use a compare-and-set rule. Otherwise a slow old refresh can overwrite a newer value. A lock alone does not solve the stale-writer problem after lease expiry.
  • Add TTL jitter to spread synchronized expirations, a global refresh concurrency cap, deadlines, and backoff after repeated failures. Jitter spreads many keys; it does not prevent one extremely hot key from stamping. Use negative caching only for explicitly safe, short-lived not-found outcomes.
  • Monitor origin QPS, refresh concurrency, hit/fresh/stale/miss rates, age served, lease contention, and refresh failures. Include tenant/permission/version context in cache keys where values differ; a fast cache must not leak another tenant's data.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• Stale-while-revalidate improves availability but requires a real product freshness allowance.
  • Distributed leases reduce duplicate work but add a dependency; local coalescing is simpler and may suffice at small scale.
  • Longer TTL improves hit rate but delays visibility; invalidation/versioning adds coordination and failure cases.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Expire the hottest key under load; confirm refresh work is bounded rather than proportional to request count.
  • Crash the lease holder, delay an old refresh beyond lease expiry, and publish a newer source version during that delay.
  • Simulate origin failure until stale-until passes; verify the app stops serving data beyond its stated freshness limit.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: What changes for rapidly changing permissions, large values, a multilevel CDN/application cache, or a backend that cannot return versions?

sections.title: Self-review rubric
sections.html:
• Bounds duplicate refreshes and waiting clients.
  • States freshness limits and handles stale writers.
  • Tests overload and failures rather than assuming a good cache hit rate is sufficient.

cards.title: Ship a change with measurable reliability
cards.question:
Design a rollout and monitoring plan for a new API implementation. The dashboard shows a stable average latency, but a small group of users experiences failures and long waits. Decide what to measure and when to stop the rollout.

Requirements

  • Define a user-centered success SLI and a latency SLI with explicit denominators.
  • Roll out gradually with a fast rollback or disable path.
  • Avoid high-cardinality telemetry labels containing arbitrary user IDs, URLs, or request bodies.

Assumed scale

Assume 10 million eligible requests/day and a 99.9% successful-request SLO over 28 days. At a steady volume, 280 million requests allow about 280,000 unsuccessful requests. A 5% failure rate burns budget 50× faster than the allowed 0.1% error rate.
cards.answer:
Define eligible requests and success precisely: for example, valid authorized requests that return a correct response before the product deadline. Separate expected client errors from service failures deliberately, rather than silently removing all 4xx or timeouts from the denominator.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Start from a user's successful interaction, not CPU utilization. Identify the population your denominator excludes.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Define eligible requests and success precisely: for example, valid authorized requests that return a correct response before the product deadline. Separate expected client errors from service failures deliberately, rather than silently removing all 4xx or timeouts from the denominator.
  • Measure latency as a distribution or as the fraction below a user-relevant threshold. A mean hides tails, and averaging per-instance p99 values does not produce a global p99. Aggregate compatible histogram buckets/counts or an appropriate distribution representation.
  • Canary the change on a small, representative traffic slice; compare success, latency, resource use, and business correctness with a control. Segment using bounded dimensions such as region, client version, and endpoint class to uncover concentrated failures.
  • Set rollback triggers before release: sustained excess errors, deadline misses, saturation, or a correctness invariant violation. Use both short and longer observation windows to distinguish a short spike from persistent budget consumption. Keep a manual stop and test the rollback path.
  • Propagate request deadlines and trace context. Use metrics for fleet-wide detection, sampled traces for causality, and structured logs for specific events. Redact sensitive data and keep a release/version marker so an incident can be correlated to the change.
  • After a rollback, preserve evidence, reduce impact, and write down the failed assumption and a prevention test. A green dashboard is insufficient if the SLI excludes the affected users or the sample is too small.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• A small canary reduces blast radius but needs enough traffic and representative cohorts to reveal failures.
  • Aggressive rollback thresholds reduce damage but can react to noise; thresholds should reflect volume and business cost.
  • More tracing helps diagnosis but adds storage/overhead and privacy exposure; sampling needs a deliberate policy.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Inject a failure limited to one region or client version; ensure segmentation catches it.
  • Cause a long-tail latency regression while holding the mean steady, and simulate missing telemetry.
  • Exercise rollback with a backward-compatible data/schema migration; verify older code can still serve safely.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: How would you handle low-traffic services, asynchronous workflows, schema changes that cannot be rolled back, or an SLO that conflicts with cost?

sections.title: Self-review rubric
sections.html:
• Defines measurable SLIs and calculates budget consumption correctly.
  • Distinguishes detection, diagnosis, and mitigation.

cards.search: Ship a change with measurable reliability SLOs & rollout Design a rollout and monitoring plan for a new API implementation. The dashboard shows a stable average latency, but a small group of users experiences failures and long waits. Decide what to measure and when to stop the rollout. Assume 10 million eligible requests/day and a 99.9% successful-request SLO over 28 days. At a steady volume, 280 million requests allow about 280,000 unsuccessful requests. A 5% failure rate burns budget 50× faster than the allowed 0.1% error rate. Define eligible requests and success precisely: for example, valid authorized requests that return a correct response before the product deadline. Separate expected client errors from service failures deliberately, rather than silently removing all 4xx or timeouts from the denominator. Measure latency as a distribution or as the fraction below a user-relevant threshold. A mean hides tails, and averaging per-instance p99 values does not produce a global p99. Aggregate compatible histogram buckets/counts or an appropriate distribution representation. Canary the change on a small, representative traffic slice; compare success, latency, resource use, and business correctness with a control. Segment using bounded dimensions such as region, client version, and endpoint class to uncover concentrated failures. Set rollback triggers before release: sustained excess errors, deadline misses, saturation, or a correctness invariant violation. Use both short and longer observation windows to distinguish a short spike from persistent budget consumption. Keep a manual stop and test the rollback path. Propagate request deadlines and trace context. Use metrics for fleet-wide detection, sampled traces for causality, and structured logs for specific events. Redact sensitive data and keep a release/version marker so an incident can be correlated to the change. After a rollback, preserve evidence, reduce impact, and write down the failed assumption and a prevention test. A green dashboard is insufficient if the SLI excludes the affected users or the sample is too small. A small canary reduces blast radius but needs enough traffic and representative cohorts to reveal failures. Aggressive rollback thresholds reduce damage but can react to noise; thresholds should reflect volume and business cost. More tracing helps diagnosis but adds storage/overhead and privacy exposure; sampling needs a deliberate policy. Inject a failure limited to one region or client version; ensure segmentation catches it. Cause a long-tail latency regression while holding the mean steady, and simulate missing telemetry. Exercise rollback with a backward-compatible data/schema migration; verify older code can still serve safely. How would you handle low-traffic services, asynchronous workflows, schema changes that cannot be rolled back, or an SLO that conflicts with cost?

cards.title: Reserve scarce inventory without overselling
cards.question:
Design a reservation API for a limited-capacity workshop. Multiple clients may reserve the last seat at the same time; clients retry and abandoned reservations expire.

Requirements

  • Never confirm more seats than capacity. A user cannot hold duplicate active reservations for the same workshop.
  • Reservation creation is retry-safe and holds expire after 10 minutes unless confirmed.
  • Explain which state changes must be atomic and how confirmation races with expiry.

Assumed scale

Assume 2 million workshops, usually under 100 seats each. Normal traffic is 300 reservation requests/s, but a popular workshop can receive 5,000 requests/s for its last few seats. Most contention is concentrated on one row/key.
cards.answer:
Choose one authoritative database transaction for the capacity invariant. A simple model locks the workshop row, checks remaining capacity, inserts a reservation with a unique business/idempotency key, and decrements remaining seats atomically. An atomic conditional UPDATE ... WHERE remaining > 0 is another valid foundation.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Write the invariant and the legal state transitions before selecting databases. Find the smallest atomic boundary that preserves them.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Choose one authoritative database transaction for the capacity invariant. A simple model locks the workshop row, checks remaining capacity, inserts a reservation with a unique business/idempotency key, and decrements remaining seats atomically. An atomic conditional UPDATE ... WHERE remaining > 0 is another valid foundation.
  • Store reservations with an explicit state such as HELD, CONFIRMED, EXPIRED, or CANCELLED, plus expires_at and an idempotency key. Enforce duplicate-active-reservation policy with an appropriate database constraint or a separate unique active-ownership row; application pre-checks alone race.
  • Confirm using a conditional state transition that verifies HELD and an unexpired deadline under the same lock/transaction policy. The expiry worker similarly changes HELD to EXPIRED and releases capacity exactly once. Whichever valid transition wins prevents the other from also releasing or confirming the seat.
  • A periodic expiry worker is not a precise timer. The confirmation path must check expiry itself, and reservation creation may reclaim expired holds transactionally if the product needs immediate reuse. Use the authoritative database time for these decisions.
  • Handle transaction serialization/deadlock failures with bounded retries and the same operation identity. Do not perform slow external calls while holding the hot row lock. Emit confirmation notifications through an outbox so notification failure does not roll back an already committed reservation.
  • Scale hot workshops by limiting admission/queueing contention before the database and making rejection fast. Sharding helps independent workshops; splitting one capacity invariant across shards requires quota allocation or stronger coordination, not just adding replicas.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• Pessimistic locking gives a clear invariant but serializes a hot workshop. Optimistic compare-and-swap may retry heavily under contention.
  • Long holds are user-friendly but reduce availability of scarce seats; short holds need clear expiry UX.
  • Read replicas can serve browsing availability approximately, but final reservation decisions must use the authoritative transaction.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Race 100 clients for one seat; exactly one hold succeeds and capacity never becomes negative.
  • Race confirmation with expiry, retry a committed reservation after a lost response, and replay the expiry job.
  • Kill workers after committing a state change, inject transaction conflicts, and verify the capacity plus held/confirmed-count invariant.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: Add multi-seat reservations, cancellation, waitlists, or reservations spanning two workshops. Which operations introduce multi-resource transactions?

sections.title: Self-review rubric
sections.html:
• Protects capacity and uniqueness with database-enforced atomicity.
  • Handles expiry/confirmation and retry races without double release.
  • Explains hot-key contention and the actual consistency requirements.
